extra.message: The `code_execution` view takes the `first_name` POST parameter, base64-decodes it and passes the result straight to `exec()`. Any unauthenticated user can POST base64-encoded Python to /injection/code-execution and obtain arbitrary code execution (full RCE) in the web server process. The bare `except` clauses only hide errors; they do not stop execution of the injected code.

extra.message: The `user_pic` view reads the `p` query parameter and passes it directly to `os.path.join(base_path, filename)` and `open(...)` with no canonicalisation, allowlist or confinement check. `os.path.join` discards `base_path` when `p` is absolute (e.g. `?p=/etc/passwd`) and `..` sequences escape the images directory (e.g. `?p=../../../settings.py`), so an unauthenticated attacker can read arbitrary files from the filesystem; the contents are returned in the HttpResponse. The `IOError` handler even coaches the attacker toward a working traversal payload.

extra.message: `dor_user_profile` reads the `userid` path segment and looks the record up directly in the `users` store (`users.get(userid)`) with no authentication and no check that the requested object belongs to the caller. Any visitor can enumerate /direct-object-references/users/<id> to read any user's name and email, and a POST to the same URL overwrites that user's name and email. The object identifier is entirely client-asserted, so this is broken object-level authorization on both the read and the write path.

extra.message: `missing_access_control` decides whether to render the privileged admin page purely from the client-supplied query parameter `action`: `if request.GET.get('action') == 'admin'` renders `access_control/admin.html`. There is no authentication check and no server-side role/permission lookup, so any anonymous user reaching /missing-access-control/happy-page?action=admin gets the administrative interface. Authorization is asserted by the client instead of by server-side identity and policy.

extra.message: `unvalidated_forward` takes the `fwd` query parameter and resolves it against the module namespace with `globals().get(forward)`, then invokes the resulting object with the request. There is no allowlist of forwardable targets, so an attacker can name any module-level callable — including the privileged `admin` view (`?fwd=admin`) or `user_pic`/`code_execution` — to reach functionality the URL configuration does not expose and bypass any front-door access control. Non-callable globals reached this way also cause unhandled type errors.

extra.message: `unvalidated_redirect` passes the raw `url` query parameter to `django.shortcuts.redirect()` without validating the scheme or host against an allowlist. A request to /redirects-and-forwards/redirect?url=https://evil.example sends the victim a 302 to an attacker-controlled site, enabling phishing and credential-harvesting that appears to originate from this trusted domain. `javascript:` style targets are similarly reflected.

extra.message: `xss_path` places the URL path segment (captured by the permissive `(?P<path>.+)` pattern in badguys/urls.py:44) into the template context, where `vulnerable/xss/path.html` renders it with the `|safe` filter inside a `<script>` block. Attacker-controlled path content is therefore injected unescaped into executing JavaScript, giving reflected XSS against any visitor who follows the crafted URL.

extra.message: `var myvar = "{{path|safe}}";` interpolates the user-controlled URL path into a JavaScript string literal with Django auto-escaping explicitly disabled via `|safe`. A payload containing a quote and `</script>` or `";` terminates the statement and executes attacker JavaScript in the victim's session.

extra.message: `DEBUG = True` (and `TEMPLATE_DEBUG = DEBUG`) is the committed default with no environment override. In this state Django serves full interactive tracebacks containing source code, local variable values, the SECRET_KEY and other settings to any client that triggers an exception, and it disables ALLOWED_HOSTS validation. Active debug functionality is directly reachable via the `/misconfiguration/boom` route.

extra.message: The `show_toolbar` callback enables django-debug-toolbar whenever the client supplies a `debug` query parameter, POST field or cookie — there is no INTERNAL_IPS or DEBUG gate. Any remote user can append `?debug=1` to a page and get the debug toolbar, which exposes settings, SQL queries, request/session contents, template context and the SQL-explain panels of a production deployment.

Because `DEBUG = True` in badguys/settings.py:10, Django responds with a full technical 500 page disclosing the traceback, source snippets, local variables, installed apps and the project's settings — including SECRET_KEY — to any anonymous requester.

extra.message: The Django `SECRET_KEY` is hardcoded in source and committed to version control. Anyone with repository access can forge signed cookies and session data, craft valid password-reset tokens and tamper with any `django.core.signing` payload, since this key is also the session/CSRF signing secret.

extra.message: `response.set_cookie(key='monster', value='omnomnomnomnom!')` sets a cookie without `httponly=True` or `secure=True`. The cookie is therefore readable by any injected JavaScript (the same view reflects unescaped input into the page) and is transmitted over plaintext HTTP, so it can be stolen via XSS or network interception.

extra.message: The profile-modification branch of `dor_user_profile` mutates another principal's stored name and email with no audit record. Neither this view, nor the privileged `missing_access_control` admin branch, nor the `unvalidated_forward` reflection path emits any security event, and the project's LOGGING configuration (badguys/settings.py:139-161) only mails unhandled 500s to admins — there is no middleware, handler or hook anywhere in the request path that records access-control decisions or sensitive state changes. Successful IDOR exploitation and privilege escalation therefore leave no durable trail for detection or forensics.
